newsitem.title: USA: Lear did not get promises from Ford for seat help.
newsitem.headline: Lear did not get promises from Ford for seat help.

text.p: Lear Corp.'s top executive said Thursday the company did not receive any promises of future business from Ford Motor Co. when it agreed to help the automaker out of a jam by supplying replacement seats for sport utility vehicles.

Ford was forced to halt production of the popular and profitable Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle when its original seat supplier, Johnson Controls Inc., was hit with strikes by the United Auto Workers union last month.
Lear Chairman Kenneth Way said his company took the action to help out a customer.

"We weren't licking our chops," Way told reporters at a briefing at the SAE International Congress and Exposition. "All we wanted to do was help the customer, break even on the deal and hopefully long-term we'll get some consideration. It's that simple."
Johnson Controls was prepared to continue making seats with non-union replacements after the strike began Jan. 28, but Ford refused to accept them. Ford continued to make Expeditions without seats.

However, when it looked like the walkout would not be settled quickly, Ford during the first week of February turned to Lear, an arch rival of Johnson Controls. Lear agreed to supply second and third row seats for the Expedition.

The dispute arose over contract terms after Ford encouraged Johnson Controls to not stand in the way of UAW organising attempts at two seat plants. It was settled last week when the company agreed to wage hikes of 20 percent to 55 percent that bring workers to approximately the $12-14 an hour that Lear pays its seat workers.

Lear is continuing to make seats for Expeditions that Ford made without seats. Way said he expected Lear to break even on the deal. Lear, which is already a major seat supplier to Ford, "probably won't know for years" how its decision to help the automaker will pay off, said Way.
"We just helped them out in this case. Maybe we're stupid. We'll find out down the road," Way said.

Nearly all of Lear's U.S. plants are unionized vs. Johnson Controls, which is predominantly non-union. Way said Lear and Ford share the same view that it is advantageous to have a positive relationship with the union.
"We plan to make the best of it," he said. "They're here to stay."

Lear is not opposing union organisation efforts at two or three of the plants that came with its Automotive Industries acquisition, said Way. He said having union workforces does not increase the company's total costs.

Although Lear sometimes pays a higher base wage than its competitors, Way said the company gets benefits from improved worker cooperation, simpler job classifications, and overall better productivity.
Way said material expenditures, which account for 70 percent of costs, are a bigger factor than wage rates.
"It's not the labour rate," he said. "It's can we be as productive as anybody else. If we can, the rate is not the issue."
